books.section: Topic 7.4 The Progressives — Theodore Roosevelt and the 'Square Deal'
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

primary_sources: Theodore Roosevelt, speech to farmers, New York (1903)

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, and 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20; verbatim excerpt (abridged) from Theodore Roosevelt's 1903 speech, public domain.
stimulus.text:
Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, and 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20: In 1902, anthracite coal miners went on strike, and President Theodore Roosevelt called both sides to the White House, threatening to take over the mines if the owners would not negotiate. The miners won a 10 percent wage increase but not union recognition. Roosevelt called the settlement a 'Square Deal.' He also used the Sherman Antitrust Act against the Northern Securities Company, a railroad holding company, and in 1904 the Supreme Court upheld the breakup.

'We must act upon the motto of all for each and each for all. ... We must see that each is given a square deal, because he is entitled to no more and should receive no less.' — Theodore Roosevelt, speech to farmers in New York, 1903 (abridged)

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9
stem: Which of the following best characterizes Roosevelt's Square Deal?

options.text: conservation, control of corporations, and protection of consumers
protective tariffs, centralized banking, and conservation
options.misconception: Tariffs and a central bank were not the Square Deal's core; Wilson later built the Federal Reserve, and tariffs belonged to other debates.

options.text: equal opportunity, women's suffrage, and laissez-faire economics
options.misconception: Laissez-faire contradicts the Square Deal entirely, and suffrage was a parallel reform, not its core.

options.text: laissez-faire economics, support of labor unions, and conservation
options.misconception: Laissez-faire contradicts the Square Deal; Roosevelt regulated business and split the difference with unions rather than backing them outright.

rationales.A: Roosevelt's program rested on three aims: conserving natural resources, controlling corporations through regulation and antitrust, and protecting consumers with laws like the meat and pure food acts. His own words, a square deal for every man, sum up the referee's stance behind all three.
rationales.B: The Federal Reserve came under Wilson in 1913, not under Roosevelt. Tariffs were not the Square Deal's defining feature.
rationales.C: Laissez-faire meant leaving business alone. The Square Deal meant regulating it, so the two cannot sit in the same answer.
rationales.D: Roosevelt was no laissez-faire president, and he did not simply back unions. He refereed between labor and business.
rationales.general:
1. Read Roosevelt's own words. Every man gets a square deal, no more and no less, whether rich or poor.
2. Match the words to the policies. Conservation saved resources, antitrust controlled corporations, and the food and meat acts protected consumers.
3. Rule out the mismatches. Tariffs, central banking, and laissez-faire belonged to other programs or the opposite idea.
Remember: a president's program is a bundle, so name all three parts before choosing.
